title: Creative Writing
summary: Learn the craft of creative writing: finding ideas and a writing habit, building characters, showing and setting, plot and structure, dialogue and point of view, poetry forms, editing and sharing your work.
audience: Aspiring writers, students, teachers and content creators

lessons.title: Finding ideas and building a writing habit

body.p: Creative writing turns experience, observation and imagination into stories, poems, scripts and personal essays. Writers are made by practice: reading widely, writing regularly and revising patiently.

list: Your own life and community: a market, a bus journey, a family celebration, a difficult choice.
"What if?" questions: What if a girl found a phone that receives tomorrow's messages?
Overheard conversations, news stories, proverbs and folk tales retold in new ways.
Objects and photographs: imagine who owned them and what happened.
Strong feelings: a moment of fear, joy, shame or wonder.

body.p: Write little and often. Writing 500 words three times a week gives 1500 words a week, enough for a short story every few weeks. Keep a notebook or phone note for ideas, phrases and observations. Read as a writer: notice how authors open stories, describe places and end chapters.

body.tip: Free-write for ten minutes without stopping or editing; it switches off the inner critic and often surprises you.

body.p: Readers care about stories because they care about characters. Memorable characters want something, face obstacles and change, or refuse to change, through the story.

list: Desire: what does the character want, and why does it matter to them?
Obstacle: what stands in the way: another person, society, nature or the character's own fear?
Contradictions: real people are mixed; a generous trader who cannot forgive her brother is more interesting than a perfectly good one.
Specific details: a habit, a way of speaking, an object they always carry.
Backstory: know more than you write; let it shape behaviour rather than explaining it all.

body.p: Reveal character through action, choices and dialogue rather than labels. Instead of writing "Kofi was brave", show him walking back into the flooded street to fetch his neighbour's goat.

body.tip: Interview your character: ask what they fear, what they lie about and what they would never do.

body.p: "Show, don't tell" means letting readers experience scenes through concrete details and action, rather than summarising feelings and facts.

list: Telling: "The market was busy and Amina felt nervous."
Showing: "Traders shouted prices over the hiss of frying plantain. Amina wiped her palms on her skirt for the third time and counted the coins again."

body.p: Go beyond sight: sound, smell, taste, touch and movement make settings vivid. Choose a few precise details rather than long lists, and pick details that reveal mood or character. Setting can shape the story: a drought, a crowded taxi rank or a quiet village at night creates different pressures and possibilities.
Figurative language (similes, metaphors, personification) can make description fresh, but avoid clichés such as "as white as snow"; find comparisons from your characters' world.

body.tip: Telling is useful for moving quickly through time; save showing for the moments that matter most.

body.p: Plot is the sequence of events shaped to create meaning and tension. Many stories follow a broad arc:

steps: Opening: introduce the character, setting and something unsettled.
Inciting incident: an event disturbs normal life and creates a goal or problem.
Rising action: attempts and complications raise the stakes.
Climax: the moment of greatest tension and decision.

list: Start close to the action; cut long introductions.
Every scene should change something: information, relationships or stakes.
Use cause and effect: "because" and "therefore" link scenes better than "and then".
Plant details early that pay off later.
End with a sense of change or meaning, not necessarily a happy ending.

body.p: Structure can also play with time: flashbacks, frame stories (a story told within a story, common in oral traditions) and multiple narrators.

body.tip: Summarise your story in one sentence: "When X happens, Y must do Z or else W." If you cannot, the plot may need focus.

lessons.title: Dialogue, voice and point of view

body.p: Good dialogue sounds natural but is sharper than real speech: it reveals character, creates conflict and moves the story forward.

list: Cut small talk unless it reveals something.
Let characters avoid, interrupt and misunderstand each other; what is not said creates tension.
Use simple dialogue tags such as "said" and "asked" and let the words carry emotion.
Reflect how characters really speak, including code-switching between languages, used with care so readers follow.
Start a new paragraph for each new speaker.
First person ("I") gives intimacy and a distinctive voice but limits what the narrator knows.
Third person limited follows one character closely.
Third person omniscient knows everything and can move between characters.
Second person ("you") is rare but can be powerful.

body.p: Voice is the personality of the writing: word choice, rhythm and attitude. It grows from writing honestly and often.

body.tip: Read your dialogue aloud; if it is awkward to say, it is awkward to read.

lessons.title: Poetry, editing and sharing your work

body.p: Poetry compresses language, using imagery, sound and form. Free verse follows the natural rhythm of speech; fixed forms set rules: a haiku has three lines of 5, 7 and 5 syllables (17 in total) and usually captures a moment in nature; a sonnet has 14 lines, often divided into 8 and 6. African oral forms such as praise poetry (izibongo, oriki) use repetition, epithets and rhythm.

list: Use concrete images rather than abstract statements.
Listen to sound: alliteration, rhyme, rhythm and repetition.
Choose line breaks deliberately to create pauses and emphasis.

steps: Revise the big picture first: structure, character, pace.
Then edit sentences: cut unnecessary words, choose precise verbs, vary sentence length.
Proofread last for spelling and punctuation.
Get feedback from trusted readers or a writing group.

body.p: Share work through school magazines, competitions, open-mic events, blogs and literary journals. Respect copyright: your original work belongs to you, and you must not copy others' writing.

body.tip: Cut your first paragraph and see if the story starts better at the second; often it does.

quiz.q: A good way to generate story ideas is to ask:
Writing 500 words three times a week gives how many words a week?
Readers care about characters mainly when they:
Which line shows rather than tells?
options: She wiped her palms on her skirt and counted the coins again.

quiz.q: Which is a cliché to avoid?
options: A fresh metaphor from the character's world
